chapters.title: Chapter 3: Pulling the Three Working Capital Levers

lessons.title: Managing Inventory: Stock Levels, Dead Stock and Cash Sitting on Shelves

children.text: Inventory is the only part of working capital that looks like success. A full godown feels like a business ready for anything, and nobody walks past it and thinks "there is ₹1.8 crore of my money, sitting still". Receivables at least have a due date. Stock has no due date at all. It sits there costing money quietly until somebody sells it, and a worrying share of it never sells at full price.

body.text: Every item in your godown was paid for with cash that could have been in the bank. Stock is not an asset you own, it is a loan you have made to your own operations, and the interest runs every single day.

children.text: What Holding Stock Actually Costs
Managers routinely assume inventory is free to hold once bought. It is not, and the total is far larger than most people guess. Here is a realistic build-up for an Indian manufacturer.

body.caption: Annual cost of carrying inventory, as a percentage of stock value

cells: Cash credit or overdraft rate, or the return the money could have earned elsewhere
Godown rent, electricity, forklifts, storekeeper salaries
Fire, flood and burglary cover on stock
Designs that go out of fashion, expiry, model changes
Roughly a fifth of the stock value, every year

body.text: That number gives procurement a break-even to negotiate against. Holding two extra months of stock costs about 3.6% of the annual spend on that item, because 21.5% a year applied to two months out of twelve is 3.58%. So a bulk discount of 5% for two extra months is worth taking, and a discount of 3% is not. Without the carrying cost, nobody in the room can tell those two deals apart.

stats.label: Konkan Ceramics inventory
stats.context: 78 days of cost of goods sold

body.title: Put a number on the godown
body.prompt: Konkan Ceramics holds ₹1.8 crore of inventory and its carrying cost is 21.5% a year. What does holding that stock cost for one year, in ₹ lakh? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹180 lakh times 0.215 is ₹38.7 lakh a year, which is about a third of the company's entire annual profit. Most of that cost never appears as a line item anyone owns. Interest sits in the finance cost, rent in overheads and obsolescence in a year-end write-off, so no one in the business sees the total.

children.text: Stock Turns: The Number to Manage
Days inventory outstanding from Lesson 2.2 has a twin that operations teams find more intuitive: how many times a year the whole godown empties and refills.

body.latex: \text{Stock turns} = \frac{\text{Cost of goods sold}}{\text{Average inventory}} \qquad \text{Days} = \frac{365}{\text{Stock turns}}
body.caption: Konkan Ceramics: ₹8.4 crore divided by ₹1.8 crore is 4.67 turns, which is 78 days

children.text: More turns on the same sales means less cash locked up. Going from 4.67 turns to 5.6 turns, which is 78 days down to 65, releases about ₹30 lakh, exactly the figure from the improvement plan in Lesson 2.2. That is the same money, seen from the operations side rather than the finance side.

body.caption: Inventory days for the year ended March 2026, as reported on screener.in
headers: Why the business needs that much

cells: Gold and finished jewellery displayed across hundreds of stores
Thousands of shades and pack sizes, made to stock, sold through a vast dealer network
Fast-moving groceries, bought cheap for cash and sold within weeks
Batch firing, wide design range, dealer-driven demand

body.text: There is no universally good number of turns. A jeweller at DMart's 37 days would have nothing in the display cases, and a grocer at Titan's 222 days would be selling expired food. Compare against your own history and your direct competitors, then ask whether each extra day of stock buys a sale you would otherwise lose.

children.text: Not All Stock Is Equal
The single most useful inventory exercise is also the least popular, because it makes a loss visible. Age the stock the way you aged receivables in Lesson 3.1.

body.title: Konkan Ceramics: inventory by age (₹ lakh)

children.text: The ₹20 lakh sitting over 180 days is the interesting pile. It is discontinued designs, shades a dealer ordered and never lifted, and tiles from a batch with a slight colour variation. Everyone in the business knows it will not sell at list price, and nobody wants to be the person who says so, because saying so creates a write-down.

body.title: Clear it now, or hold on hoping?

columns.label: Clear it at half price today
points: ₹10 lakh of cash arrives this month
Godown space freed for stock that moves
The loss is recognised once, cleanly
Bank sees a smaller but healthier stock statement

columns.label: Hold it another year
points: About ₹4.3 lakh of carrying cost on ₹20 lakh
The realisable value keeps falling as designs age
The write-down still comes, just later and bigger
Working capital limits stay tied up against stock that is not selling

body.text: The cash test cuts through the emotion. Ask one question about any slow-moving item: if I did not already own this, would I buy it today at its book value? If the answer is no, the money is already lost. Clearing it simply decides how much you recover and how soon.

body.title: The operations metric
body.textWithBlank: Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory gives the number of stock ___ in a year.
body.explanation: Higher turns mean the same sales are supported by less stock, so less cash is locked up. Turns and inventory days are two views of one number: 365 divided by turns gives the days.

children.text: Where Indian Businesses Over-Stock
Excess inventory is rarely a storekeeping failure. It is usually the accumulated residue of reasonable-sounding decisions taken elsewhere in the business.
Minimum order quantities.
A supplier will not sell less than a full container or a full batch, so six months of an input arrives at once.
Import lead times.
Sea freight of 30 to 45 days plus customs means importers hold far more stock than domestic buyers, and every delay adds a safety buffer.
Price-rise buying.
Steel, copper or crude-linked inputs are expected to rise, so procurement buys ahead. Sometimes correct, often an expensive bet funded by the bank.
Festive and seasonal build-up.
Diwali stock built in August, monsoon stocking before transport gets difficult, March-end push to hit annual targets.
Sales forecasts nobody owns.
Optimistic forecasts become production plans, production plans become finished goods, and the finished goods become next year's slow-moving stock.
Fear of stock-outs.
One angry dealer call is remembered far longer than the ₹38 lakh a year the extra safety stock costs to hold.

body.title: Stock-outs cost money too, so how much buffer is right?

children.text: This lesson is not an argument for running dry. A stock-out costs the margin on the lost sale, and sometimes the customer. The judgement is a trade-off, and it can be made numerically per item rather than by instinct for the whole godown.
Cost of holding:
about 21.5% a year on the value of the buffer stock.
Cost of a stock-out:
the lost gross margin, plus the risk that a dealer switches supplier permanently.
The rule that follows:
hold generous buffers on cheap, fast-moving, hard-to-substitute items, and thin buffers on expensive, slow-moving items that customers will wait for.

That is the practical heart of ABC analysis and reorder levels, which are covered in depth in our working capital course. For cash purposes, what matters is that a blanket policy such as "always hold two months of everything" guarantees you overpay on the expensive items and still run out of the cheap ones.

Two arrangements worth asking about, both common in India: consignment stock, where the supplier owns the goods sitting in your godown until you consume them, and vendor managed inventory, where the supplier monitors your levels and replenishes. Both move the carrying cost to whoever can bear it most cheaply.

body.title: Which stock reduction releases the most cash safely?
body.question: Konkan Ceramics wants to release cash from inventory without risking sales. Which action fits?
options: Halve the stock of its fastest-moving, lowest-value clay input, which is delivered locally within two days
Clear the ₹20 lakh of designs older than 180 days, and stop producing the three slowest-moving designs
Cut the finished goods of its best-selling tile, which dealers order every week
Delay the next glaze shipment, which has a 45-day sea lead time and no domestic alternative
body.explanation: Dead and slow-moving stock is cash that is already impaired, so releasing it costs no sales at all. The other three all cut stock that actively supports revenue, and the glaze in particular has a long lead time and no substitute, which is exactly where a buffer is worth its carrying cost.

body.title: The container that saves 8%
body.scenario: Konkan Ceramics buys ₹2.6 crore of glaze and chemicals a year, currently holding about one month of stock. Procurement has found an import route: buy in full containers, three months at a time, and the landed cost falls 8%. Sea lead time is about 45 days. The head of procurement points out the saving is ₹20.8 lakh a year and wants sign-off this week.
body.prompt: Work out the real economics, then decide.
body.modelAnswer:
Do the cash arithmetic first.
1. The saving is real: 8% of ₹2.6 crore is ₹20.8 lakh a year.
2. Stock goes from one month, about ₹21.7 lakh, to three months, about ₹65 lakh. That locks up an extra ₹43.3 lakh of cash, permanently, for as long as the policy runs.
3. At a 21.5% carrying cost, holding that extra stock costs about ₹9.3 lakh a year.
4. Net benefit, on these numbers, is about ₹11.5 lakh a year. The deal is genuinely positive, which is why it deserves a serious answer rather than a reflex no.
Now the risks that the ₹11.5 lakh does not capture.
5. Where does the ₹43.3 lakh come from? If the cash credit limit is already stretched, the answer is that it comes out of paying suppliers on time, and Lesson 3.2 explains what that costs.
6. Currency risk. Imports priced in dollars can move several percent before the container lands, and 8% of margin is not a large buffer against that.
7. Lead time risk. A 45-day sea route plus customs means a quality problem is discovered ten weeks after ordering, with three months of the defective batch in the godown.
8. Obsolescence. If a glaze is tied to specific designs, three months of it is only an asset while those designs sell.
What I would approve.
9. Yes in principle, but start with a single container and a two-month holding, not three, and measure the actual landed cost including finance and freight.
10. Ask the supplier for staggered dispatch against a committed annual volume, which often captures most of the discount without the stock.
11. Confirm the cash is available without touching supplier payments, and put a hedge in place if the exposure is material.
12. Review after two cycles with real numbers, and agree upfront what would make us reverse the decision.

body.title: Run a dead stock review this month
steps: Pull a stock listing with the last issue or sale date for every item, not just quantities and values.
Flag everything untouched for more than 180 days, and everything with less than one sale in the period.
For each flagged item ask the honest question: would we buy this today at book value?
Get a realistic clearance price from sales, not a hoped-for one.
Compare the cash from clearing now against the carrying cost of another year plus the likely further fall in value.
Take the write-down in one decision rather than a slice each year, and make sure the bank and the auditors see a consistent story.
Fix the cause, not just the symptom: the forecast, the minimum order quantity or the design range that created the item in the first place.
Check that stock statements submitted to the bank reflect the cleaned-up position, since drawing power is calculated on them, as Chapter 5 explains.

cards.definition: The annual cost of holding stock: funding, storage, insurance, damage and obsolescence. Often around a fifth of stock value.
Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. How many times the godown empties and refills in a year.
Items that will not sell at book value. Cash already spent, where the only decision left is how much to recover.
A deliberate buffer held against demand and lead time uncertainty. Worth its cost on cheap, fast-moving, hard-to-substitute items.
Goods held in your godown but owned by the supplier until consumed, so the carrying cost sits with them.
The smallest quantity a supplier will sell. A common reason businesses hold far more stock than they need.

points: Holding stock costs roughly 21.5% a year once funding, storage, insurance, damage and obsolescence are added up.
Konkan Ceramics spends about ₹38.7 lakh a year holding ₹1.8 crore of stock, roughly a third of its profit, and no single manager sees that cost.
Stock turns and inventory days are the same number. Moving from 4.67 turns to 5.6 releases about ₹30 lakh.
Age your inventory as you age receivables. Dead stock is cash already lost, and clearing it only decides how much comes back.
Over-stocking usually comes from minimum order quantities, import lead times, price-rise buying, seasonal build-up and unowned forecasts.
Bulk discounts must be netted against carrying cost. Two extra months of stock costs about 3.6% of annual spend, so any discount below that destroys value and anything above it is worth examining.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional, and the carrying cost components are typical illustrative rates, not a benchmark for any specific business. Titan, Asian Paints and DMart figures are from screener.in as published at the time of writing and may be restated. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation on any security.
